newsitem.title: USA: No decision on first day of Food Lion deliberations.
newsitem.headline: No decision on first day of Food Lion deliberations.

text.p: Jurors deliberated for more than five hours Tuesday but reached no decision on whether the ABC television network should be ordered to pay punitive damages to supermarket giant Food Lion Inc. for an undercover report about food safety.

The report broadcast on "PrimeTime Live" in 1992 claimed that Salisbury, N.C.-based Food Lion sold spoiled meat and used unsanitary food handling practices. Food Lion's stock price and store sales plunged for several weeks following the broadcast report.
U.S. District Judge Carlton Tilley read his instructions to the panel and shortly after 10 a.m. EST and jurors were given a 12-page verdict sheet to complete as part of their deliberations.
The panel met for five and a half hours on its first day of deliberations. It was scheduled to resume deliberations at 9:30 a.m. Wednesday.

The punitive damage phase of the trial means the jurors must decide if ABC, its former parent company Capital Cities/ABC Inc., one executive producer and one senior producer of "Prime Time Live" and two undercover journalists should be ordered to pay damages to Food Lion. Capital Cities/ABC was bought last year by Walt Disney Co. for $19 billion.

The jury's deliberations will be made somewhat more complicated by the fact that one of the undercover journalists worked at a Food Lion store in South Carolina, which has a different standard for the the burden of proof than required under North Carolina law, lawyers said.

The case is being closely watched by U.S. media organizations as a litmus test of whether companies can sue for investigative reports that executives dislike. Instead of pursuing a libel claim against ABC, Food Lion attacked the way the story was obtained by the journalists with hidden cameras.
Tilley instructed jurors that punitive damages were to be awarded solely to punish the defendants for their conduct and to deter others from engaging in similar conduct.

"If you decide, in your discretion, to award punitive damages, any amount you award must bear a reasonable relationship to the nature and expense of that defendant's conduct and the harm or injury which it caused," Tilley said.
The judge told jurors that they must assume all information in the Nov. 5, 1992 "PrimeTime Live" program was true, including the video pictures of spoiled meat and unsafe food repackaged for sale.
During trial testimony last month, ABC said it earned $58,970 in profits on the "PrimeTime Live" show about Food Lion. But the grocery store chain claimed the network earned much more than that.

The jury hearing the case in U.S. District Court in Greensboro, N.C., found last month that ABC committed fraud when two producers went to work undercover at Food Lion and awarded the grocer $1,400 in compensatory damages.
Although Food Lion did not ask jurors to order a specific amount in punitive damages, attorneys for the company urged the panel on Monday to order "very large" damages against ABC.
Food Lion attorney Timothy Barber said the punitive damages should be large enough to stop news organizations from pursuing future investigative reports that break the law in the process.
Barber said Monday that jurors might want to consider taking away Capital Cities/ABC's profits for the number of days that the ABC undercover investigation lasted.

He told jurors that with annual profits of $1.3 billion, ABC last year made a daily profit of about $3.5 million. That amount, multiplied by the 60-day investigation, would total some $210 million, Barber said in his example to jurors.

The grocery store chain also suggested that the two executive producers of the program, Ira Rosen and Richard Kaplan, each be ordered to pay $50,000 in punitive damages. Food Lion also urged jurors to order the two producers to pay an amount proportionate to their salaries.
Disney's stock closed up $1.25 at $69.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
